chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
title: Musicians' politics, voting and the presidents
summary: Crawford says the musicians took little interest in politics or voting until Roosevelt, and he praises Truman and Carter.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Were many musicians very aware of politics and stuff in those days? Did they talk much about presidents prejudice?
No, because most of the people in
the South, the colored people, they were Republicans. No Democrats around (Inaudible). I just found that out (inaudible).
Did many musicians vote, register to vote and stuff?
No, not our men. Of course, now I vote in every election.
What about Smith? Did Willie Smith vote? Or Lunceford?

Not that I know of, no. Up until Roosevelt, I think that opened their eyes quite a bit, opened their eyes quite a bit, because that man did quite a bit. People like President Abraham Lincoln, who was an abolitionist, that's why they killed him, get him out of the way.
Well, some people say that's why they think they killed Huey Long, too, because he was doing some of these programs --
Yeah, some of these programs were helping --
Yeah, that's what some people think.
Well, he was a pretty liberal-minded man. Even though he was a staunch Southerner. People like FDR and that President Truman, beautiful man. He'd stand on

his rights, and he was a liberal-minded President, him. Roosevelt and Truman and Carter, the present President. Now, I'm hoping and praying to God nothing will ever happen to him, because these damn bigots, you never know. He'll come out in the open and tell you, he's a Baptist, also. Black and whites, what's the difference?
